title: Seven climate terms fitted on 1902-1996 explained at most 28% of the 2010-2024 runoff deficit at 32 south-east Australian gauges; a post hoc linear decline fitted on the same years predicted all of it
abstract:
Question: after 1997, south-east Australian (SE-AU) runoff fell below each catchment's rainfall-runoff relation and stayed low. Long records (bundle 4e9ae7e7) show that runoff efficiency also changed before 1997. Is this multi-decadal change caused by a measurable climate driver, and does a driver fitted only on years before 1997 predict the post-1997 deficit?

Approach: 32 SE-AU and 19 northern control gauges (Bureau of Meteorology flow, SILO rain, 1902-2024). Per gauge, annual runoff in % of mean flow = a + bP + cP(t-1) + dX, with d pooled over each region and all fits on 1902-1996 only. Seven terms X were set in a plan before any residual: IPO tripole index (annual and 13-year phase), Indian Ocean Dipole, CRU TS maximum temperature and potential evaporation, cool-season rain share, rain of years t-2 to t-6. Tests: leave-one-block-out R2 of 13-17-year block departures before 1997, and the explained part of the 1997-2009 and 2010-2024 departures. 2-degree cell bootstrap.

Results: observed SE-AU departures were -8.7% (95% CI -17.3 to -2.5) in 1997-2009 and -16.1% (-23.2 to -10.7) in 2010-2024. No term passed the planned rules. The highest block R2 was 0.21. Only the cool-season rain share explained a clear part of the 2010-2024 deficit (28%, -4.5 points, -6.7 to -2.3). Maximum temperature explained 37% with an interval that includes 0. The IPO predicted higher runoff after 1997 in both regions (wrong sign). Post hoc: the temperature effect disappeared when a time trend was added; the efficiency fall near 1957 (16 points) came with 0.3 C of warming. A linear decline fitted on 1902-1996 (-3.3% of mean flow per decade, -4.6 to -1.6) predicted -16.0% (-21.8 to -7.7) for 2010-2024; a 1957 step or the 1977-1996 level predicted only -5% and -4%. Pre-1997 13-year lows were within stationary AR(1) noise (P = 0.59), but the 1997-2024 mean was not (P = 0.006).

Conclusion: the tested climate terms do not explain the century-scale change in runoff efficiency. The post-1997 deficit is consistent with the continuation of a slow decline since the early 20th century, not with an IPO phase or a unique drought shift. The trend is a post hoc description, not a cause.

Limitations: few gauges before 1940; annual linear models; the trend and other post hoc tests were chosen after the planned results; the northern trend forecast failed after 2009.
